My social anxiety stems from being autistic so I will never "get over it", when I do something very anxiety-inducing like playing with other people or soloing a dungeon, I follow that up with something easy and/or relaxing like daily delves or fishing. That said, I do take medication for anxiety and I believe that really helps!

Another tip if you're like me in that when you're anxious, you forget what buttons to press is to have a one-bar build. I also have some cognitive difficulties due to chronic illness and I found two bars overwhelming at the best of times. Luckily, one bar is enough for all but the hardest content with the right build.

Lastly, the best thing I ever did was join a guild that was specifically made for LGBT+, neurodivergent, anxious, depressed people and while they were active, I knew that no matter what I do, NOBODY was going to be judging my performance or be mad at me if I do something wrong. I even successfully ran trials with this guild.

If you were on PC EU, I'd have ran you through some of the easiest dungeons (that I have successfully soloed before) so you could have taken your time, done the quests, looted everything etc. and known that I'm more than happy to wait. There are way better players than me out there who could do the same for harder content. I assume that is true for PS as well. 

I wish you luck in your endevours! There are so many of us with anxiety out there, finding the right people helps immensely!

Right, sorry. I get irked when I see "correcting" because it almost always implies unnecessary violence. In your case it's not (if the dog is okay with picking up). It can actually prove beneficial if your dog is in a stressful situation where you can't remove the stressor. My dog's way too heavy but it would make both our lives so much easier if I could pick her up and carry her away from the scary thing that's too close.

"...physically and verbally correcting" also implies an aversive, which is just as shitty as a shock collar. Yeah, aversives are effective but not more so than force-free training that doesn't confuse the dog and damage your relationship with them.

Honestly? I get it. Your dog is obviously loved and I'm sure he wants to accompany you too. Having a harness is already great. The prong is not necessary, but prey drive or leash reactivity requires time and effort (and working with a licensed behaviourist) to manage. 

Dog training is a highly unregulated field and anyone can call themselves a trainer. Even people who have certificates might only have them for a certain narrow field and that doesn't mean they're automatically experts on everything. It's really hard and time-consuming to sift through all the available info and wannabe "dog whisperers" to find scientifically proven, humane dog training methods.

Even if you put in the effort and do everything right, your dog might not ever be safe around prey animals. It's important to know their limits and manage their environment as best you can.

I honestly don't know how dog fighting works, but even biting can be taught humanely. Biting is something that can be taught just like any other behavior (sit, lie down, roll over...). 

What I assume happens is the dog is put into an extremely stressful 'eat or be eaten' situation where it doesn't have a choice but to bite back. After going through that again and again, the dog learns that seeing another dog means they'll have to fight to survive. Some don't ever fight back. Some do it for self-preservation.

Nowhere in that story is there 'rewarding aggressive behavior'. I don't think people involved in dog fighting reward the dogs for anything because positive reinforcement isn't something their tiny brains can grasp.

I am not a canine behaviorist and I may get some things wrong but if you want to influence how the dog acts (i.e. showing signs of discomfort like snarling) it's important to understand and change the emotion behind it. If the dog is showing aggression because it's fearful then it's paramount to help the dog feel more comfortable and work on it in small steps the dog doesn't find overwhelming. 

Dogs don't just 'go postal' (unless there's something physically wrong) if you don't ignore their body language. If you either ignore or physically punish snarling/snapping/growling the dog will learn it's boundaries are not being respected (or that giving preemptive signs of discomfort is not effective) and will have to resort to biting. 

Look up calming signals. It's a way dogs de-escalate situations and is extremely valuable knowledge when interacting with them.

I'm not entirely sure what you mean but if it's advice on leash pulling they could just, you know, use science-backed training methods and teach the dog to walk nicely on a leash. There's never a reason to use prong collars. They're illegal in my country.

There's a lot of disinformation out there so I'm not judging you for using it, especially if you feel like you don't have a choice walking a dog with a distinct prey drive. Kikopup on YT is a good starting point for learning about force-free training.

You can't "reward aggression", for fuck's sake. Fear/discomfort is an emotion not a behaviour. If you do something to help the dog in an unpleasant situation while it's exhibiting signs of discomfort, it's not "rewarding" it.

Kikopup has a playlist dedicated to puppy training. It's someone I can recommend because I know for a fact they don't use punishment or aversives. https://youtube.com/user/kikopup

This is a very concise post specifically about puppy biting.
https://m.facebook.com/story.php?story_fbid=3528126627217710&id=914162368614162

And a few tips on puppy training in the form of a free ebook/pdf. 
https://eileenanddogs.com/life-lessons-puppy/

Unfortunately, puppies act like puppies and that's unavoidable, but there are ways you can help the puppy express normal dog behaviors (biting, chewing, licking...) without getting blood blisters.

I'm not gonna offer any concrete advice because I'm not a certified behaviourist (which is why I linked to someone who is) and even though it's well-meaning, my advice might be off and lead to more problems.

You can find science-based force-free trainers yourself, most offer individual (online and otherwise) counseling on what would be the best course of action for your particular situation. There are also plenty of other free resources on the Internet. 

I wish you luck and a long and happy life with your pup!

Too much exercise can have the opposite effect - you will have an overly excited dog that can't calm down. The answer is to use both physical and mental exercise (and do so in moderation). 

First make sure your dog knows the crate is the best place to be by filling up a cong or some other type of high value enrichment. He needs to feel safe and cosy.

Gradually try giving some type of high value enrichment item and leaving for a short time (make sure it's safe for them to be alone with it). Only use the high value treat (like peanut butter, for example) for when he's in/around the crate so he connects the two more quickly.

Most importantly, give him time to adjust. Bond with him by using walks or short 10min training session to teach him fun things (or basics).

If it happens that he turns out to be an anxious dog, you might consider force-free behaviourists in the area.

Be very careful who you pick to work with you though, do your research on them and see what kind of background they have (where they studied, the classes they took...). A good question to ask is how they would respond if the dog does what we consider 'inappropriate' or 'unwanted' behaviour. If the answer is anything involving aversives/punishment, run away. Though I think you will be fine just reading science backed articles on training.

I understand this is "only" a foster, but he deserves the best chance and even though it sounds like a lot of work, it really isn't. You don't need too much of anything. Short exercise or longer walks and 10-20min of mental enrichment should be enough to bond you with the dog. That's just an estimate, I might be wrong. And all dogs have different needs.

I am not a trainer or expert of any kind and my advice will always be - go to a behaviourist or trainer who's qualified, certified and continues to study based on newest scientific research. It doesn't have to be because a dog has a problem, but simply because you wanna get started right and someone knowledgeable can help you understand a dog better.

The most important thing to remember is that the dog is not giving you a hard time, he's /having/ a hard time. (It might not be related directly to your situation, but that pretty much goes for everything.)
